cues.text: A Family of Scholars
Born around 950 near Lake Van , in the Armenian kingdom of Vaspurakan (in what is now eastern Turkey), Gregory came from a family devoted to Church learning.
His father, Khosrov, was a bishop and theologian who authored one of the earliest commentaries on the Armenian Divine Liturgy.
After his mother's early death, Gregory and his brothers were raised by their uncle Anania, founder and abbot of the Narek Monastery .
A Life Confined to One Monastery

Gregory entered monastic life at Narek as a young man and, remarkably, spent almost the whole of his life within its walls, ordained a priest around age twenty-five and teaching at its monastic school.

His era was a genuine golden age for Armenian culture — a flourishing of literature, art, architecture, and theology in the decades before Turkic and Mongol invasions would later devastate the region.
The Book of Lamentations
Gregory's masterwork, completed the year before his death, is his Book of Lamentations (Narek) , ninety-five extended mystical prayers exploring the soul's longing for reconciliation with God.
Asked once how anyone could offer anything meaningful to a Creator who already possesses and knows everything, Gregory answered simply: “the sighs of the heart.”
This was the spirit in which he composed his entire book.
He himself described it as described as “an encyclopedia of prayer for all nations”
A Beloved and Enduring Text
The Book of Lamentations became, and remains, one of the most treasured works in all of Armenian literature and devotion.
For centuries, Armenian families kept copies in their homes, some regarding the book as a source of spiritual consolation and healing.
It has since been translated into some thirty languages.
Many of Gregory's hymns and prayers are still sung in Armenian liturgies today.
Death and Destruction of Narek
Gregory died at Narek Monastery around 1003 and was buried within its walls.
A chapel-mausoleum marked his tomb for centuries, until the monastery was destroyed in the early twentieth century amid the Armenian Genocide .
The monastery had stood for over a thousand years, and the monastery's buildings were destroyed, and the site was subsequently used for other purposes.
Legacy: A Doctor for a Wounded People
In 2015, on the hundredth anniversary of the Armenian Genocide, Pope Francis declared Gregory of Narek a Doctor of the Church .
This was a striking gesture of unity toward the Armenian Apostolic Church, from which Gregory himself came.
It also recognized a mystical voice that had helped sustain Armenian faith and identity through centuries of hardship and, in the twentieth century, unimaginable suffering.
